slides.title: Starter Activity: 6-Cell Knowledge Retrieval

starterQuestions.q: Convert 350 nm into micrometres (µm) in standard form.
Calculate percentage change if resting heart rate is 65 bpm and peak post-exercise is 143 bpm.
What is the mathematical distinction between interpolation and extrapolation?
starterQuestions.a: Interpolation estimates values within the range of collected data points; extrapolation predicts values beyond the measured experimental boundaries.

starterQuestions.q: Why is extrapolation risky when modelling human physiological recovery curves?
starterQuestions.a: Physiological responses are governed by non-linear homeostatic feedback, enzymatic saturation, and recovery limits, so trends rarely stay linear.

starterQuestions.q: What happens to the Surface Area-to-Volume (SA:V) ratio as cell radius increases?
starterQuestions.a: The SA:V ratio decreases because volume scales with radius cubed (r³) while surface area scales with radius squared (r²).

starterQuestions.q: State the standard metric unit for cardiac frequency.
starterQuestions.a: Beats per minute (bpm) or Hertz (Hz = beats per second).

slides.title: Slide 7
slides.text:
Key Diy Deliverable Workshop & Step-by-Step Practical
Live Data Collection: Resting vs. Post-Exercise Cardiovascular Response
Step 1: Baseline Acquisition
©) Measure and record resting heart rate (bpm) for 3 minutes to establish a reliable baseline. Ensure
absolute adherence to P4 safety protocols (informed consent, clear workspace).
Step 2: Physiological Stress Test
Ne) Subject performs 3 minutes of controlled cardiovascular exercise (e.g., step-ups). Record heart rate
immediately upon cessation (Minute 0), and then every 60 seconds for 5 minutes during recovery.
Step 3: Enterprise Data Plotting
4 Plot raw data on standardized axes (Time on X-axis, Heart Rate on Y-axis). Calibrate your scale
meticulously. Draw a smooth curve or line of best fit (never dot-to-dot) to secure Distinction criteria (D2).
Step 4: Interpolation & Extrapolation Output
Using a ruler, interpolate the estimated heart rate at exactly 2 minutes 30 seconds of recovery. Then,
extend your trend line to tentatively extrapolate when the heart rate will return to the exact resting baseline.
